note: Tyler Shough might have crapped the bed from a real-life standpoint last week, but he has continued to cook from a fantasy standpoint as the QB3 in fantasy points per game. The only quarterbacks with more fantasy points per game than Shough this season are Josh Allen and Brock Purdy. Wild. Among 31 qualifying passers, Shough is 11th in passing success rate, 13th in highly accurate throw rate, and third in hero throw rate. Shough should still rack up the stats this week, but it won't be easy. Atlanta has allowed the eighth-fewest yards per attempt, the sixth-lowest passing success rate, and the 14th-fewest EPA per dropback. Atlanta also has the second-best pressure rate and the fifth-best quick pressure rate. Shough has navigated pressure well this season with the ninth-best yards per attempt and the fifth-best passing success rate against pressure.

Dak Prescott is the QB8 in fantasy points per game. Among 31 qualifying quarterbacks, Prescott is eighth in passing success rate, second in highly accurate throw rate, seventh in catchable target rate, and he has the ninth-lowest off-target rate. Prescott is also 13th in fantasy points per dropback. Prescott should turn in another QB1 performance this week against a struggling Houston pass defense. The Texans have allowed the seventh-highest yards per attempt, the eighth-highest passer rating, and the third-highest CPOE. Prescott should have clean pockets against a pass defense that surprisingly has the second-lowest pressure rate and the fifth-lowest quick pressure rate.

Well, I was worried about it. Bryce Young finally came back to earth last week as the QB22 for fantasy. Young's deeper metrics made me worry about this, and they don't look any better after Week 3. Among 31 qualifying passers, he's seventh in yards per attempt, ninth in hero throw rate, and has the fourth-highest deep ball rate, but he also has the fourth-lowest highly accurate throw rate, the lowest catchable target rate, and the ninth-highest off-target rate. Young is attempting to walk a weekly tightrope of a volatile but high-upside deep-ball passer. There will be boom weeks and big-time down weeks if he continues to live in this world all season. Luckily for Young, the Lions are a very accommodating opponent for this style of play and should allow for a bounce back this week. Detroit has allowed the ninth-most yards per attempt, the third-highest passing success rate, and the sixth-highest CPOE. The Lions have also struggled with defending the deep ball, giving up the fourth-highest deep ball completion rate and passing success rate downfield.

Well, Kyler Murray's first game as Minny's starter didn't go great. He was the QB27 in weekly scoring last week. Yes, I know Justin Jefferson got banged up last week, which no doubt impacted Murray's day. That doesn't mean that we can excuse his performance. After last week, among 38 qualifying passers, Murray has the third-lowest yards per attempt, the lowest passing success rate, the lowest highly accurate throw rate, and the fourth-lowest catchable target rate. WOOF! Murray also ran only twice for 17 yards. None of this will get the job done, but maybe Miami is the magic elixir for Murray in Week 4. Miami has allowed the second-most yards per attempt, the fourth-highest passer rating, the highest passing success rate, and the most fantasy points per dropback to quarterbacks. Murray could look revitalized for at least one week.

Jordan Love is the QB17 in fantasy points per game with one QB1 (QB11) outing in weekly scoring this season. Love has been rattled all season behind his patchwork offensive line, which the Packers are attempting to band-aid together after signing nearly every free-agent offensive-line option with a pulse this week. Among 31 qualifying passers, Love has the fourth-lowest passing success rate, the 11th-lowest yards per attempt, the lowest highly accurate throw rate, and the second-highest off-target rate. I'm not saying that Love will be amazing this week, but the Bucs pass defense isn't one that I fear. Their season-long metrics are being propped up by the fact that they have faced Deshaun Watson and Kyler Murray over the last two weeks. Yes, they have allowed the 13th-lowest CPOE, the 12th-fewest fantasy points per dropback, and the 13th-lowest EPA per dropback, but again they have faced Watson and Murray in two of three games in this sample. The Bucs also have the fourth-lowest pressure rate and the 11th-lowest quick pressure rate. If the new additions to the Green Bay line can help buy Love any more time this week, he could surprise.

Drake Maye has looked like a turnover-prone shell of his 2025 self to begin this season as the QB36 in fantasy points per game. Among 31 qualifying passers, Maye has the sixth-lowest passing success rate and the highest turnover-worthy throw rate while ranking 16th in highly accurate throw rate and 17th in catchable target rate. He also hasn't run enough weekly to save his fantasy value, with more than 20 rushing yards in only one game. Maybe this is the "get right" spot for Maye, but at this point I gotta see it to believe it. Buffalo has allowed the 11th-most yards per attempt, the seventh-highest passing success rate, and the 11th-highest CPOE.

C.J. Stroud is the QB15 in fantasy points per game, but he has been struggling as a passer to begin the 2026 season. Among 31 qualifying passers, Stroud has the tenth-fewest yards per attempt, the 12th-lowest passing success rate, the tenth-lowest catchable target rate, and the fifth-fewest fantasy points per dropback. Stroud has further proven so far that his rookie season is the outlier in his NFL resume. As bad as Stroud has been, Dallas might prop him up this week. Stroud could post solid QB2 numbers this week against Dallas's underwhelming pass defense. Dallas has allowed the 12th-most yards per attempt and the second-highest EPA per dropback and passing success rate.

After his bellyflop in Week 1, Matthew Stafford has been a strong QB1 with QB6 and QB9 finishes in weekly scoring. Since Week 2, among 28 qualifying passers, Stafford ranks fifth in yards per attempt, seventh in fantasy points per dropback, 17th in highly accurate throw rate, and 15th in catchable target rate. Stafford could post QB1 numbers again this week against an up-and-down Philly pass defense. Philly has allowed the 11th-fewest yards per attempt and the tenth-lowest passing success rate, but they have also surrendered the eighth-most EPA per dropback and rank 18th in CPOE permitted. Philly has the sixth-lowest pressure rate this season, so Stafford should have time in the pocket to find the holes in the Eagles' coverage.

Bo Nix has looked like a backup quarterback for most of the season. It has been tough to watch. Among 31 qualifying passers, Nix has the ninth-fewest yards per attempt, the sixth-lowest passing success rate, the tenth-lowest highly accurate throw rate, the seventh-lowest catchable target rate, and the third-highest turnover-worthy throw rate. Yep, it has been THAT BAD. I don't see Nix turning it around this week. The 49ers have allowed the seventh-fewest yards per attempt, the 11th-lowest CPOE, and the third-fewest fantasy points per dropback.

Last week, Marcus Mariota surprised everyone as the QB13 for the week, as he was highly efficient with three passing scores against Seattle. Mariota added only five rushing attempts and 11 yards on the ground. Among 31 qualifying passers this season, Mariota is seventh-best in passing success rate, sixth in passer rating, eighth in catchable target rate, and first in hero throw rate. I expect him to add more rushing this season as Washington's starter. Mariota could flirt with QB1 production again this week against a pass defense that has allowed the fifth-most EPA per dropback, the third-most yards per attempt, and the eighth-highest passing success rate. Jayden Daniels returned to practice this week, but I would be shocked if he played this week.

Jacoby Brissett is the QB20 in fantasy points per game with a QB4 performance in weekly scoring last week. Among 31 qualifying passers, he has been a quick-passing point guard with the lowest time to throw, the fourth-lowest aDOT, and the third-fewest yards per attempt. Brissett also has the fourth-fewest fantasy points per dropback while ranking 13th in passing success rate. Brissett should have another strong QB2 performance with the upside to flirt with QB1 production this week. New York has allowed the 14th-highest passing success rate, the seventh-highest CPOE, the tenth-most fantasy points per dropback, and the sixth-most EPA per dropback.

Daniel Jones has struggled to open the season as the QB34 in fantasy points per game. Jones hasn't eclipsed 13 fantasy points in any start this season. Among 31 qualifying passers, Jones has the sixth-fewest yards per attempt, the 14th-lowest passing success rate, the fourth-lowest CPOE, the fifth-lowest aDOT, and the 12th-highest off-target rate. Jones has been BAD. I don't have a ton of faith in Jones, but the matchup is glorious this week. Maybe he flashes a fantasy pulse this week as a decent QB2. Washington has allowed the fifth-most yards per attempt, the most passing touchdowns, the sixth-highest passing success rate, and the fourth-most EPA per dropback.

Last week, in his first game back, Sam Darnold was forced to air it out, and he finished as the QB2 for the week. Darnold finished with 379 passing yards and four passing touchdowns (two picks). Among 38 qualifying passers, he ranks sixth in yards per attempt, 13th in passing success rate, 26th in highly accurate throw rate, fourth in catchable target rate, and seventh in fantasy points per dropback. Darnold should follow it up with another solid fantasy showing against a Bolts pass defense that has allowed the seventh-most yards per attempt, the fifth-highest passing success rate, and the ninth-most EPA per dropback.

Geno Smith is the QB19 in fantasy points per game after last week's fantasy point explosion as the QB3 for the week. Smith has had a mini renaissance to begin this season. Among 31 qualifying passers, he is eighth in yards per attempt, tenth in passing success rate, second in catchable target rate, and 11th in hero throw rate. The Bears look like a tough assignment on paper, but through three games they got lit up by Bryce Young and then had good outings against Carson Wentz and a struggling Jalen Hurts. I'm not scared of this pass defense despite allowing the ninth-lowest passing success rate, the seventh-fewest EPA per dropback, and the fifth-lowest CPOE. Chicago has the tenth-lowest pressure rate. I expect Smith to have time to pick apart this pass defense in Week 4. Smith is a solid QB2 who could flirt with QB1 production again this week.

Justin Herbert and the Chargers offense have been one of the biggest disappointments through three games. Herbert is the QB32 in fantasy points per game without a single game with more than 15 fantasy points. Among 31 qualifying passers, Herbert has the 14th-fewest yards per attempt, the seventh-fewest fantasy points per dropback, the eighth-lowest passing success rate, and the fifth-lowest EPA per dropback. I don't see this being the week that Herbert turns things around against this vaunted Seattle pass defense. Seattle has allowed the fewest yards per attempt, the seventh-lowest passing success rate, and the sixth-fewest fantasy points per dropback.

Kirko Chainz has the Raiders undefeated as the QB11 in fantasy points per game. Yes, I'm as surprised as you are by that last statement. Cousins has been playing good football. Among 31 qualifying passers, he ranks 16th in yards per attempt, 14th in passing success rate, 18th in highly accurate throw rate, and ninth in catchable target rate. He'll have his hands full with a surprisingly stout Chiefs' pass defense. Kansas City has allowed the third-fewest yards per attempt, the fourth-lowest passing success rate, and the fourth-lowest CPOE. While Spags has been in his bag with the coverages, he has only been able to muster the 15th-best quick pressure rate while standing at 13th-best in pressure rate. Cousins will have to operate quickly with the ball in his hands this week.

In his first game back under center, Michael Penix was the QB20 in fantasy. Among 30 qualifying quarterbacks last week, he was third in yards per attempt, 12th in passing success rate, and 13th in catchable target rate while having the third-lowest aDOT (6.41). Penix should have another solid starting outing in Week 4 against a Saints pass defense that has allowed the ninth-highest passer rating, the fourth-highest passing success rate, and the 12th-most EPA per dropback. Penix should have clean pockets to work from, as the Saints have the ninth-lowest pressure rate and the 12th-lowest quick pressure rate.

In weekly fantasy scoring, Deshaun Watson has finished as the QB21, QB12, and QB14. Watson has added some rushing equity with eight rushing attempts and 35 yards on the ground per game. He has continued to struggle as a passer, as a low aDOT point guard. Among 31 qualifying passers, Watson has the second-lowest aDOT, the 14th-lowest catchable target rate, the eighth-highest off-target rate, and the fifth-highest turnover-worthy throw rate. Watson has the fourth-highest percentage of his passing yards that have come from YAC (59.1%). Watson could have another passable QB2 week against a Steelers pass defense that has allowed the tenth-most yards per attempt, the 11th-highest passing success rate, and the ninth-highest CPOE.

The falloff had to come at some point, but it appears here for Jameis Winston. Over the last two games, he has been the QB32 and QB31 in weekly fantasy scoring. I think it's just a matter of time before we see JJ McCarthy making starts for the Giants. Among 31 qualifying passers, Winston has the lowest yards per attempt, the lowest passing success rate, the fifth-lowest highly accurate throw rate, and the fourth-lowest catchable target rate. I'm not playing Winston. I don't care about the matchup.

Aaron Rodgers had a mini renaissance last week as the QB7 in fantasy. Overall, he is the QB27 in fantasy points per game, with only that performance as his claim to fantasy fame for 2026 as a QB1. Among 31 qualifying quarterbacks, Rodgers has the fifth-lowest yards per attempt, the 11th-lowest passing success rate, the sixth-lowest catchable target rate, and the 12th-lowest hero throw rate. Rodgers will likely return to the QB2 ranks this week against a pass defense that has allowed the 13th-fewest yards per attempt while ranking 16th in passing success rate and EPA per dropback allowed. The key for Cleveland this week is for their pass rush, which is third in pressure rate and fourth in quick pressure rate, to get home. If it does, Rodgers will have trouble, as he has the 12th-fewest yards per attempt and the tenth-lowest passing success rate when under pressure this season.

With Baker Mayfield out, Jalon Daniels will draw the start for the Bucs this week. The dual-threat rookie has some rushing upside, with at least 404 rushing yards and four scores on the ground in each of his final three collegiate seasons. My comp for him as a prospect was Tyler Huntley. He could provide similar output as the Bucs starter. During the preseason, Daniels ran 14 times, churning out 37 rushing yards. Among 70 qualifying passers in the preseason, he was only 48th in yards per attempt, 30th in adjusted completion rate, and 37th in big-time throw rate (per PFF). During his final collegiate season, among all FBS quarterbacks with at least 150 dropbacks, Daniels was 76th in adjusted completion rate, 40th in yards per attempt, and 33rd in big-time throw rate. Daniels could return decent QB2 production this week if he does utilize his legs in the rushing department. The Packers are a middle-of-the-road pass defense, ranking 17th in CPOE, 16th in fantasy points per dropback, and allowing the 14th-most yards per attempt.

Through three games this season, Malik Willis has finished as the QB13, QB22, and QB28 in weekly fantasy scoring. In two of those games, he has been rushing like we hoped, averaging 7.5 rushing attempts and 47.5 rushing yards. Willis hasn't been great as a passer despite flashing his arm talent at times. Among 31 qualifying passers, he ranks 13th in yards per attempt and sixth in hero throw rate, but he also has the fifth-lowest catchable target rate and the third-highest off-target rate. Willis will need all the rushing equity he can get this week to save his fantasy day. Minnesota's defense has been nasty. They have allowed the fourth-fewest passing touchdowns, the lowest passer rating, and the lowest passing success rate. The Vikings also have the sixth-best pressure rate and the ninth-best quick pressure rate. Good luck, Willis.

Cam Ward has been a miserable disappointment this season as the QB27 in fantasy points per game. I was worried about Ward this preseason as the all-22 film scared the crap out of me. Nothing Ward has done in the regular season has made me feel any better. Among 31 qualifying passers, Ward has the fourth-fewest yards per attempt, the ninth-lowest CPOE and passing success rate, the second-lowest highly accurate throw rate, and the eighth-highest turnover-worthy throw rate. I don't see Ward turning his season around this week. Baltimore has allowed the ninth-fewest yards per attempt, the 13th-lowest passing success rate, and the fourth-fewest fantasy points per dropback. Ward is a sit weekly until he shows some glimmer of hope.

Case Keenum started for Chicago last week despite Tyson Bagent clearing the concussion protocol. I expect Bagent to start for Chicago this week, but that isn't for certain. I'll update this situation as we get more info. I expect Caleb Williams to be sidelined again this week.

Chuba Hubbard is Carolina's bell cow. Hubbard is the RB9 in fantasy points per game. Last week, he was the RB12 for the week. Hubbard finished with 23 touches and 110 total yards. Hubbard had an 83% snap rate, 82.6% of the rushing attempts, a 66.7% route share, and an 8.3% target share. Among 43 qualifying backs, he is 11th in explosive run rate and 14th in yards after contact per attempt. Hubbard should be a locked-in RB1 again this week. Detroit has allowed the highest explosive run rate, the 11th-highest rushing success rate, and the third-most yards before contact per attempt.

Aaron Jones is battling through a banged-up knee. Last week, despite the less-than-full-strength knee, Jones played 81.8% of the snaps with 73.9% of the rushing attempts, a 58.8% route share, and a 20.7% target share. Jones finished with 22 touches and 92 total yards. I don't know how long he'll hold up to this workload, but fantasy gamers should appreciate it while we have it. Among 43 qualifying rushers, Jones is 34th in explosive run rate, 37th in yards after contact per attempt, and 34th in missed tackle rate. None of those numbers surprise me at all. Jones is essentially Alvin Kamara of the North now. Jones is a volume-based RB2/flex again this week. Miami ranks 18th in explosive run rate, 17th in missed tackle rate, and has allowed the third-fewest yards before contact per attempt.

D'Andre Swift has been crushing it as the RB7 in fantasy points per game, averaging 20.7 touches and 107 total yards. Among 43 qualifying backs, Swift is eighth in yards after contact per attempt and tenth in missed tackle rate. Swift has 14 of the team's 20 running back red zone carries while playing 64.1% of the snaps with a 51.4% rushing share, a 35.7% route share, and a 9.2% target share. Swift should have another strong stat line this week against a Jets' run defense that has allowed the second-highest rushing success rate, the tenth-most yards before contact per attempt, and the third-highest missed tackle rate.

Cam Skattebo is the RB20 in fantasy points per game, averaging 19 touches and 78.3 total yards. Skattebo has a 65.7% snap rate, a 54.9% rushing share, a 48.9% route share, and a 9.6% target share. Among 43 qualifying backs, Skattebo ranks 19th in yards after contact per attempt and 12th in missed tackle rate. Skattebo should have another nice stat line this week. Arizona has allowed the fourth-highest explosive run rate, the third-most yards after contact per attempt, and the second-highest missed tackle rate.

Bucky Irving missed part of Week 3's action with a glute injury. He opened this week with a limited practice session. I don't trust Todd Bowles and injury reporting. I'll update his outlook on Friday.

Bhayshul Tuten is the RB16 in fantasy points per game, averaging 16 touches and 80 total yards. Among 42 qualifying running backs, he ranks tenth in explosive run rate, eighth in rushing success rate, tenth in yards after contact per attempt, and ninth in missed tackle rate. Among the same sample, Tuten is only 27th in snap rate and 24th in designed carry share. If he keeps producing like this on a per-touch basis, he will earn more of the Jags backfield. Tuten has six red zone carries to Chris Rodriguez's five through three games. He's had a consistent 31.3-35.5% route share (6.2% target share, 1.24 YPRR). This could be the week when Tuten finally logs a 100-yard rushing outing. Cincy has allowed the ninth-highest explosive run rate, the ninth-most yards after contact per attempt, and the seventh-highest missed tackle rate.

Braelon Allen will be New York's lead back this week. Last week, Breece Hall sustained his quad injury in the fourth quarter. In the fourth quarter, Allen played 72% of the snaps with a 50% rushing share, a 52.6% route share, and a 17.6% target share. Allen has never been the most efficient rusher, and that is the case again this season. Allen has zero explosive runs, with 1.89 yards after contact per attempt and a 16% missed tackle rate. Allen could easily see 15-plus touches this week and return RB2 production despite his inefficiencies. Chicago hasn't been able to stop the run this season, allowing the ninth-highest explosive run rate, the highest rushing success rate, and the most yards before contact per attempt.

Well, this sucks. I expected David Montgomery to be Houston's workhorse back this season, and over the last two weeks that hasn't happened. Since Week 2, Montgomery has had a 57.8% snap rate with 43.6% of the rushing attempts, a 44.1% route share, and a 4.8% target share. In these two games, he has averaged 10.5 touches and 36 total yards. This is barely flex-worthy volume behind a horrid offensive line. Montgomery hasn't been efficient with his workload so far, though. He has only a 3% explosive run rate, 1.57 yards after contact per attempt, and a 14% missed tackle rate. None of that is good. At all. Montgomery has another nice matchup this week, but he wasn't able to do anything with last week's solid matchup, so I don't know if he'll be able to take advantage this week. Dallas has allowed the third-highest explosive run rate, the seventh-highest rushing success rate, and the eighth-most yards before contact per attempt.

Quinshon Judkins has been an uninspiring volume-based flex play as the RB29 in fantasy points per game. He has averaged 17 touches and 59 total yards. Among 42 qualifying rushers, Judkins has the seventh-lowest explosive run rate while ranking 29th in yards after contact per attempt and 21st in missed tackle rate. Judkins will put up another snoozer stat line this week against a Pittsburgh run defense that has the tenth-best stuff rate while allowing the seventh-lowest rushing success rate and the 12th-lowest missed tackle rate.

Omarion Hampton has been a big letdown through three games as the RB23 in fantasy points per game. His usage trends are also going in a frightening direction, sadly. From Week 1 to last week, Hampton's designed carry share has dropped from 75% to 57.7%, and his route share has declined from 28.6% to 15.8%. There's nothing to like about any of that. Last week, Hampton finished with 15 touches and 56 total yards. In two of three games this season, he has had 15 touches or less. Among 43 qualifying backs, Hampton is 24th in explosive run rate, ninth in yards after contact per attempt, and 21st in missed tackle rate. With his route share declining and only a 3.4% target share this season, Hampton can easily be game-scripted out weekly if his usage continues to sit in this area code. That easily could happen this week against Seattle. The Seahawks' run defense also is no joke, as they have allowed the third-lowest explosive run rate, the third-lowest rushing success rate, and the sixth-lowest missed tackle rate. Hampton will need a touchdown to pay off this week for fantasy.

Last week, Rhamondre Stevenson was reinstalled as the team's lead back with a 55% snap rate and a 51.4% route share. Stevenson split the early down load with TreVeyon Henderson with a 26.9% rushing share, and each back got one red zone rushing attempt. Stevenson finished with ten touches and 38 total yards. Among 43 qualifying backs, Stevenson ranks 12th in yards after contact per attempt and 27th in missed tackle rate. Stevenson could take back more of the backfield this week if he can hold onto the ball. The Bills' run defense has been pliable, allowing the 12th-highest explosive run rate, the 12th-highest rushing success rate, and the sixth-highest missed tackle rate.

Jacory Croskey-Merritt is the RB34 in fantasy points per game, averaging 16.7 touches and 49 total yards. Bill has been a zero in the passing game with only one target in each game. He has five of the team's 11 running back red zone rushing attempts. Bill has a 47.2% snap rate with 49% of the team's rushing attempts, a 22.6% route share, and a 3% target share. All of his value in fantasy is tied to what he can do on early downs. Among 43 qualifying backs, he ranks 39th in explosive run rate, 35th in yards before contact per attempt, 31st in yards after contact per attempt, and 41st in missed tackle rate. His offensive line is giving him zero chances, as he has the second-highest rate of being hit at or behind the line of scrimmage. A porous Indy run defense might allow him some room to scamper this week. Indy has allowed the 11th-highest explosive run rate, the fourth-highest rushing success rate, the fifth-most yards before contact per attempt, and the fourth-highest missed tackle rate. Bill is a solid flex play this week who could return RB2 value if he gets in the end zone.

Alvin Kamara looks to be New Orleans' lead back while Travis Etienne is sidelined with a hamstring injury. Last week, after Etienne was out of the game in the fourth quarter, Kamara played 55% of the snaps, handled 71.4% of the rushing attempts, had a 46.2% route share, and zero targets. Kamara will be a volume play weekly. He hasn't been efficient or explosive this season with only a 5.6% explosive run rate, 1.78 yards after contact per attempt, and a 6% missed tackle rate. I expect Kendre Miller to work in on early downs so Kamara isn't asked to handle too many touches. Kamara is an unsexy volume flex this week with a bad matchup. Atlanta has allowed the lowest explosive run rate, the fifth-lowest missed tackle rate, and the have the fourth-best stuff rate.

Well, after one game, TreVeyon Henderson returned to his 1B role in the New England backfield. Last week, Henderson finished with nine touches and 29 total yards while having a 33.3% snap rate, a 30.8% rushing share, and a 27% route share (3.2% target share). Henderson has gotten off to a disappointing start again this season on a per-touch basis. Among 43 qualifying backs, he is 27th in explosive run rate, 42nd in yards after contact per attempt, and 39th in missed tackle rate. It's not difficult to understand why Henderson can't seem to grasp or hold the lead back role in New England. Rhamondre Stevenson has been the better rusher over the last two seasons. Even in an ancillary role, Henderson is an interesting flex play this week. If he can pop one of his signature long runs for a touchdown, he could pay off this week. The Bills' run defense has been pliable, allowing the 12th-highest explosive run rate, the 12th-highest rushing success rate, and the sixth-highest missed tackle rate.

Tony Pollard has taken over as Tennessee's lead back over the last two weeks. He has averaged 18 touches and 80.5 total yards while having a 53.7% snap share, 62% of the rushing attempts, a 33.3% route share, and an 8.9% target share. He's been stellar on a per-touch basis. Among 43 qualifying rushers, Pollard is ninth in explosive run rate and seventh in yards after contact per attempt. Last week, Pollard was the RB16 for the week. He could flirt with low-end RB2 production this week, but is best viewed as a nice flex play. Baltimore has allowed the sixth-highest explosive run rate, the 13th-most yards before contact per attempt, and the seventh-highest gap rushing success rate (Pollard: 65.8% gap runs).

RJ Harvey remains Denver's passing-down back. In his two games of action this season, he has had a 42.1% snap rate, only 12.5% of the rushing attempts, a 44.1% route share, and a 17.7% target share (2.31 YPRR). Harvey has averaged 7.5 touches and 44 total yards. Harvey is a middling PPR flex again this week. The 49ers have allowed the ninth-most receiving fantasy points per game to backs, but they have also held them to the sixth-fewest yards per target.

J.K. Dobbins remains Denver's early down hammer. In Weeks 1 and 3, Dobbins had a 46.7% snap rate, 62.5% of the rushing attempts, a 14.7% route share, and a 3.2% target share. In those games, he averaged 13 touches and 44.5 total yards. The biggest worry for Dobbins (outside of his touchdown-or-bust role) has been his inefficiency as a runner. Dobbins has only a 6.7% explosive run rate and a 6% missed tackle rate. These are horrible per-touch metrics for the explosive early down option for Denver. I don't see Dobbins improving those numbers this week. The 49ers have allowed the second-lowest explosive run rate, the sixth-fewest yards after contact per attempt, and the tenth-lowest missed tackle rate.

Last week, Jadarian Price was parked on the bench by Seattle after he fumbled for the second time in his last two games. Price played only 28.4% of the offensive snaps, finishing with six touches and 22 total yards. Seattle continues to split up the work for this backfield. Price isn't doing himself any favors, and until we get a clearer picture of the usage of all the backs for this team, everyone on the running back depth chart is a sit. Last week, Price, Emanuel Wilson, and George Holani all had at least a 25% snap share and a 19.1% route share. The backfield was a disgusting three-way committee and could remain that way for most of the season.

Woody Marks has made this Houston backfield into a committee. I didn't see that coming this offseason. Over the last two weeks, Marks has had a 41.4% snap rate, 33.3% of the rushing attempts, a 34.4% route share, and an 8.4% target share. Marks has averaged 9.5 touches and 28 total yards. Marks has had only 1.64 yards after contact per attempt, but he has also posted a stellar 27% missed tackle rate. Marks is a viable flex this week if you're in a pinch. Dallas has allowed the third-highest explosive run rate, the seventh-highest rushing success rate, and the eighth-most yards before contact per attempt.

Kyle Monangai is a serviceable flex again this week. Monangai has averaged 11.3 touches and 71 total yards while logging a 36.4% snap rate, 28.6% of the rushing attempts, a 26.1% route share, and a 4.1% target share. Monangai has six of 20 running back red zone carries for Chicago. Among 43 qualifying backs, he is first in yards after contact per attempt and 15th in missed tackle rate. The Jets have allowed the second-highest rushing success rate, the tenth-most yards before contact per attempt, and the third-highest missed tackle rate.

Jaylen Wright missed last week's game with a foot injury. Wright opened this week with a limited practice. Ollie Gordon operated as Miami's workhorse last week after De'Von Achane sustained a torn ACL and Wright was out. Wright returning could be the fly in the Ollie Gordon ointment for Week 4. I'll update the outlook of this backfield on Friday.

Blake Corum is a low-end flex play again this week. Corum has averaged 10.3 touches and 53.3 total yards. He doesn't have a red zone carry so far this season, so his touchdown equity is limited at best. Also, he has only five targets this season, so his value is entirely dependent upon what he does on early downs and the possibility of him breaking off a long run for score. Corum has the talent to do so, but this isn't likely the best matchup for that to happen this week. Among 43 qualifying backs, Corum ranks fourth in explosive run rate and sixth in missed tackle rate. Philly's run defense has tightened up, allowing the 13th-lowest explosive run rate, the 12th-lowest rushing success rate, and the tenth-fewest yards before contact per attempt.

Bucky Irving missed part of Week 3's action with a glute injury. Irving opened this week with a limited practice session. I don't trust Todd Bowles and injury reporting. I'll update Kenneth Gainwell's outlook on Friday. If Irving misses this week, I would expect Gainwell to lead the way for the Bucs backfield.
Rachaad White sustained a shoulder injury last week. He opened this week with a DNP. I'll update his Week 4 outlook on Friday.

Jaylen Wright missed last week's game with a foot injury. He opened this week with a limited practice. I'll update the outlook for this backfield on Friday, but Wright's return could toss a wrench in the gears for Ollie Gordon stans.
Breece Hall sustained a quad injury last week. I'm expecting him to be out this week. He opened the week with a DNP.

Tetairoa McMillan is the WR38 in fantasy points per game. He has an 18% target share, 1.60 YPRR, four red zone targets, five deep targets, and a 22.5% first-read share. The usage has been there for McMillan, but Young's volatile nature has had him riding a rollercoaster, with only 54.5% of his targets deemed catchable. This week, McMillan faces a Detroit secondary that has utilized the tenth-highest single-high rate (54.5%). This season, against single high, McMillan has seen more of the usage move in Jalen Coker's direction, as he has only a 17% target-per-route run rate and 1.00 YPRR against single high, but last year he had a 26% target-per-route run rate and 2.05 YPRR against single high. McMillan could see the usage move back in his direction this week, but there's also a runout where Coker remains the go-to guy this week. McMillan's range of outcomes is wide, but it could be fruitful this week. Detroit has allowed the sixth-most yards per target and the ninth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Well, apparently I prematurely forecasted Rashee Rice's demise after two lackluster weeks to open the season as the Chiefs' fourth target option. Last week, that changed massively. Rice led the team with a 37.5% target share, finishing with a 7.3 aDOT, 88 receiving yards (4.89 YPRR), two red zone targets, and a 38.9% first-read share (led the team by a WIDE margin). We'll see if Rice continues to see this alpha-type usage moving forward, but it was wonderful to witness if you roster Rice. This week, Rice will face a Raiders' secondary that has utilized two high with 57.5% (11th-highest rate) of their defensive snaps. Against two high, Rice leads the team with a 21% target per route run rate while posting a stellar 2.45 YPRR. Rice should see enough volume to overcome a surprisingly tough matchup this week. The Raiders have allowed the fewest yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Josh Downs is the WR33 in fantasy points per game, but he has produced much better than that fantasy ranking on a per-route basis. Downs has a 24.5% target share with 2.07 YPRR, four red zone targets, three deep targets, and a team-leading 31.5% first-read share. Downs has a stellar 0.133 first downs per route run. Downs should have another nice week against the Commanders, who since 2025 have allowed the second-most yards per target and the 12th-most fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers.

Matthew Golden is in the midst of a sophomore breakout season. Golden is the WR15 in fantasy points per game with a 22.6% target share, 2.32 YPRR, four red zone targets, six deep targets, and a 27.4% first-read share (leads the team). He has been absolutely awesome. I didn't know what to make of Golden this summer after a sleepy rookie season and minimal usage. This week, he'll face a Bucs secondary that has the second-highest single high rate in the NFL (71.7%). Against single high, he is second on the team with a 24% target-per-route run rate with only 1.43 YPRR. He has been the team's go-to against two high, with improved efficiency. This isn't a coffin nail, but it's harder to project a ceiling week for Golden when considering this. Tampa Bay hasn't been amazing at defending perimeter wide receivers, allowing the 13th-most yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to the position. Golden can still have a strong Week 4, even if he doesn't blow the doors off.

Jaylen Waddle is the WR38 in fantasy points per game, as he has suffered through bad quarterback play and questionable play calling through three games. Over the last two games, Waddle has had a 26.2% target share, 3.08 YPRR, one red zone target, four deep targets, and a 35.1% first-read share. This week, he faces a 49ers secondary that has utilized single high at the eighth-highest rate (57.7%). Since Week 2, against single high, Waddle has had a 40% target-per-route-run rate and 3.32 YPRR. That's insane usage and production. If Nix can get his head on straight, Waddle should have a banner week. The 49ers have allowed the third-most yards per target and the fourth-most fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers. Waddle was seen in a boot (foot) leaving last week's game, but he practiced in full to open this week.

Michael Wilson is the clear number two option in the Arizona passing attack as the WR21 in fantasy points per game. Wilson has a 25.6% target share with 1.38 YPRR, five red zone targets, three deep targets, and a 35.1% first-read share (leads the team). Wilson should have another productive outing in Week 4 against a secondary that has allowed the 11th-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers, while ranking 18th in yards per target given up to the position.

Last week, Malik Nabers was back to a full workload with an 81% snap rate, a 76.9% route share, a 27.3% target share, only 26 receiving yards (1.30 YPRR), and a 37.5% first-read share (one red zone target). The result wasn't amazing, but it's great to see Nabers back to a full-time role. Now, he just needs better quarterback play on the field to turn this type of market share into on-field production. Nabers should at least see enough catchable targets this week to take advantage of a nice matchup. The Cards have allowed the most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

DJ Moore has been an elite alpha in his two full games played with 16.8 PPR points per game. Overall, that would be the WR10 in fantasy points per game. In those two games, Moore has had ELITE usage and production with a 30.9% target share, 3.55 YPRR, two red zone targets, four deep targets, 0.170 FD/RR, and a 33.3% first-read share. I'm mentioning Moore here because this week he possibly gets a shadow from Christian Gonzalez, but in most weeks he is a set-and-forget must-start. This season, Christian Gonzalez has followed DK Metcalf, Jaxson Smith-Njigba, and Brian Thomas following them on 50-86.4% of their routes. Smith-Njigba roasted him, but Gonzalez held Metcalf and Thomas under 30 receiving yards in his coverage with zero scores. Moore will still be peppered with targets this week, so I'm not saying to sit him, but just temper your expectations a bit.

Well, we finally got to see the Luther Burden that was promised last week. He finished as the WR13 for the week. It looks like Ben Johnson bought all of his summer stock for Burden back. Burden has a 23.5% target share with 1.95 YPRR, six red zone targets (leads the team), zero deep targets, and a 32.8% first-read share (leads the team). This week, he faces a Jets' secondary that has the fifth-highest two-high rate in the NFL (65.4%). Against two high, Burden is second on the team with a 21% target-per-route run rate with only 0.79 YPRR. Last week, against two high, he had a 36% target per route run rate (led the team). I'm not worried about the small-sample inefficiency against two high, as he had 1.88 YPRR against two high last year with a 25% target-per-route run rate. Burden should have another busy game in Week 4 against a secondary that has ranked 15th in yards per target against slot receivers.

Terry McLaurin is the WR37 in fantasy points per game, with his best showing of the season last week as the WR14 in weekly scoring. McLaurin is tied for the team lead with a 22% target share, 1.40 YPRR, two red zone targets, four deep targets, and a 28.4% first-read share (leads the team). This week, McLaurin faces an Indy pass defense that has utilized single high at the ninth-highest rate (57.1%). Since 2024, against single high, McLaurin has had a 23% target-per-route run rate and 2.37 YPRR. McLaurin is set up to crush again this week against a pass defense that has allowed the most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per opportunity to receivers.

Stefon Diggs has had a strong start to his Washington tenure as the WR17 in fantasy points per game. Diggs is tied for the team lead with a 22% target share while producing 1.82 YPRR with four red zone targets (leads the team), three deep targets, and a 25.4% first-read share (second on the team). This week, Diggs faces an Indy pass defense that has utilized single high at the ninth-highest rate (57.1%). This season, against single high, Diggs has had a 30% target-per-route run rate and 2.19 YPRR. Diggs is a strong fantasy option this week against a pass defense that has allowed the most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per opportunity to receivers.

Justin Jefferson picked up an ankle injury last week. He opened the week with a DNP. I'll update Jordan Addison's outlook on Friday when we have more info about Jefferson. Addison could be operating as Minny's WR1 this week if Jefferson can't go.

The Chargers' passing attack is a confounding mess. It's difficult to feel good about playing anyone on that roster right now. Ladd McConkey came out of the gate hot in Week 1 until he snapped a rib, and he has been middling ever since. Last week, McConkey had a 14.7% target share (third on the team) with a 19% first-read share (third on the team). He was a full-time player, though, with an 87.5% snap rate and 84.2% route share. It's maddening. It feels like Mike McDaniel is scrambling in real time to make this all work and flailing while doing so. McConkey is second on the team in red zone targets (two) and deep targets (two). McConkey could lead the team in targets this week, or he could be the third option in the passing progressions. Who knows. I do know that I don't want to plug him into a lineup this week against a secondary that has allowed the fourth-fewest yards per target and the tenth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Deebo Samuel is the WR22 in fantasy points per game, seeing a 13.3% target share with 2.84 YPRR, three red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 14% first-read share. He has been the clear fourth option in the passing attack for San Francisco. Denver has mostly held receivers in check this season, but with Samuel's multifaceted role (four rushing attempts, 30 rushing yards) and Brock Purdy playing out of his mind, he's a flex option this week. Denver has allowed the 14th-most yards per target to wide receivers while holding them to the tenth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity.

DK Metcalf has started the season slowly as the WR47 in fantasy points per game. Metcalf has a 20.9% target share with only 0.82 YPRR, seven deep targets, one red zone target, and a 31.4% first-read share. He has seen solid volume weekly and done very little with it. Last week, he scored a touchdown as DJ Turner ran into a teammate, thus leaving Metcalf wide open in the end zone. This week, he faces a Cleveland pass defense that has the highest single-high rate (75.7%) in the NFL. Against single high, Metcalf has struggled this season with only a 19% target per route run rate and 0.61 YPRR. I expect another disappointing stat line from Metcalf this week. After their Week 1 debacle, the Browns' secondary has tightened up, allowing the seventh-fewest yards per target and the fifth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers over the last two weeks.

Oh, the yearly struggle with rostering Jameson Williams. He's the WR57 in fantasy points per game this season, and it has been a bumpy ride. Williams has a 10% target share, 1.19 YPRR, zero red zone targets, one deep target, and a 14% first-read share. I don't know if Williams' struggles are resolved this week. Carolina has the fifth-highest single high rate in the NFL (63.5%). Williams has been an afterthought against single high this season with an 11% target-per-route run rate and 0.70 YPRR. It's possible that he does bounce back this week, though. Last year, Williams had a 22% target-per-route run rate and 2.31 YPRR against single high. Carolina has been tough against perimeter wide receivers, but they just lost Jaycee Horn, so take these numbers with a grain of salt. Carolina has allowed the sixth-fewest yards per target and fourth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers. Williams is a volatile flex play this week, but his ceiling is sky-high if his usage changes against a matchup that isn't as scary as it seems on paper.

Devaughn Vele was due for a down week, and it happened last week, but he is still the WR23 in fantasy points per game. Vele has a 16.7% target share with 1.32 YPRR, three red zone targets, four deep targets, and a 20.4% first-read share. Vele faces an Atlanta secondary that has utilized single high at the fifth-highest rate (64.7%). Against single high, Vele has an 18% target-per-route run rate and a strong 1.91 YPRR. Vele is a solid flex play with a tough matchup. Atlanta has held slot receivers to the fifth-fewest yards per target and the second-fewest fantasy points per opportunity this season.

Keenan Allen might be the WR41 in fantasy points per game, but he is coming off his best showing of the season as the WR19 in weekly scoring last week. Allen has a 20.4% target share (third on the team) with 1.37 YPRR, three red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 26% first-read share (second on the team). Allen could follow up last week's performance with another nice stat line this week. Washington has allowed the fifth-most yards per target and the second-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers this season.

Jakobi Meyers is the WR30 in fantasy points per game with two top-30 finishes in weekly scoring through three games (WR28, WR14). Meyers has a 13.6% target share, 1.89 YPRR, two red zone targets (two scores), one deep target, and a 17.2% first-read share. I expect DJ Turner to follow Brian Thomas Jr. this week, but after seeing Thomas Jr.'s role in the offense decline last week, I could be wrong. Meyers could see Turner this week, so there's volatility in his projection. Turner has shadowed in each game this season following Emeka Egbuka, Xavier Hutchinson, and DK Metcalf on 53.1-69% of their routes. Turner hasn't allowed any of these receivers to surpass 53 receiving yards in his coverage. Metcalf scored a touchdown against him, but Turner ran into a teammate on the play, which left Metcalf wide open. Meyers is downgraded this week with a possible shadow and the fact that Cincy has been tough against perimeter wide receivers, allowing the second-fewest yards per target and the fourth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

Malik Washington has been a volume-filled low-end flex play this season as the WR48 in fantasy points per game. Washington has a 26.7% target share, 1.65 YPRR, one red zone target, six deep targets, and a 26.7% first-read share. Despite this high-volume usage, Washington hasn't eclipsed 12 PPR points in any game this season. This isn't the week to decide to flex him. Minnesota has allowed the ninth-fewest yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers.

Emeka Egbuka is the WR33 in fantasy points per game, but the lack of production isn't his fault necessarily. Only 65% of his targets have been catchable. Among 86 qualifying receivers, Egbuka ranks 19th in separation and 15th in route win rate, so he's doing exactly what he's supposed to be doing. Getting open early and often. Egbuka has a 20.2% target share with 1.48 YPRR, two red zone targets, three deep targets, and a 24.6% first-read share. This week, he faces a Green Bay pass defense that has the sixth-highest two-high rate (64.4%). Against two high, Egbuka has led the team with a 21% target-per-route run rate and 1.92 YPRR. If rookie Jalon Daniels can get him the ball, Egbuka could surprise people this week against a secondary that has allowed the 12th-most yards per target and the sixth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

With Cam Ward struggling to provide even league-average quarterback play, Carnell Tate has been the WR49 in fantasy points per game. Tate has a team-leading 22.7% target share with 1.46 YPRR, one red zone target, one deep target, and a 31% first-read share. Until Ward shows some promise, Tate will continue to struggle to post nice stat lines. Baltimore isn't the place to look to plug him into a fantasy lineup. The Ravens have limited perimeter wide receivers to the tenth-fewest yards per target and eighth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity.

Denzel Boston finally wasn't able to overcome his struggling quarterback last week, producing only 8.1 PPR points. Overall, he is the WR19 in fantasy points per game. Boston has an 18.1% target share, 2.27 YPRR, three red zone targets, four deep targets, and a 21.4% first-read share (second on the team). Boston could overcome Deshaun Watson's struggles again this week if he sees catchable targets. The Steelers have allowed the fourth-most yards per target and the fifth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

After a down Week 3, Dontayvion Wicks has slipped to WR32 in fantasy points per game. Wicks has a 17% target share, 2.29 YPRR, four red zone targets, four deep targets, and a 23.2% first-read share. After a dip last week, Wicks saw his route share bounce back to 77.4% last week. We'll see if Wicks can bounce back this week after a disappointing stat line against the Bears. This week, he'll tangle with a Rams pass defense that has featured two high with 58.3-60% of their defensive snaps in two of their three games. Against two high, Wicks has a 21% target-per-route run rate and 2.91 YPRR. Wicks is a solid flex play again this week. The Rams have held perimeter receivers to the 14th-fewest yards per target, but they have also allowed the 12th-most fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

Last week, Wan'Dale Robinson had easily his best showing of the season as the WR18 for the week. Robinson's issues have also been tied to Cam Ward. Robinson has a 20.5% target share with 1.33 YPRR, three red zone targets, one deep target, and a 27.6% first-read share (second on the team). Robinson could be a decent PPR or volume-based flex this week. Baltimore has allowed the ninth-most yards per target and the 12th-most fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers.

KC Concepcion is the WR69 in fantasy points per game, despite leading the Browns with a 22.9% target share. Sadly, with their struggling quarterback, Concepcion has only 1.01 YPRR, two red zone targets, and a deep target while leading the team with a 30.4% first-read share. Concepcion is likely a low-end flex play again this week against a Pittsburgh secondary that ranks 16th in yards per target allowed to slot receivers while also giving up the eighth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

Over the last two games, Doubs has been the WR23 and WR54 in weekly scoring with a 15.1% target share, 3.22 YPRR, one red zone target, one deep target, and a 14.7% first-read share. This hasn't been the usage anyone was hoping for with AJ Brown out of the lineup. We could see Doubs bounce back this week, though. It's possible that he sees shadow coverage from Christian Benford, but I doubt that Buffalo is concerned enough with Doubs to put Benford on him. Doubs could be the go-to for Drake Maye this week against Buffalo's two-high coverage. Buffalo has the tenth-highest two-high rate (58.1%). Since Week 2, against two-high, Doubs has been the leader in target-per-route run rate with 22% and 6.13 YPRR(!!). Since 2025, Doubs has seen a boost against two high with a 21% target-per-route run rate and 2.16 YPRR. If Benford doesn't follow Doubs, he should have a strong game this week. Buffalo is 15th in yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity allowed to perimeter wide receivers.

Rome Odunze has been the forgotten man in Chicago's passing attack as the WR58 in fantasy points per game. Odunze has only a 13.3% target share with 1.72 YPRR, two red zone targets, five deep targets, and a 13.1% first-read share. This week, he faces a Jets' secondary that has the fifth-highest two-high rate in the NFL (65.4%). Against two-high, Odunze's target-per-route run rate drops from 18% to 14%, and his yards per route run dips from 2.00 to 1.38. Odunze is only a middling flex play this week against a secondary that has allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 17th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed.

Courtland Sutton has started VERY slowly as Bo Nix struggles to support anyone in this passing attack week-to-week. Sutton is the WR80 in fantasy points per game with only a 16.1% target share, 1.04 YPRR, five red zone targets, two deep targets, and a 21.6% first-read share. This week, he faces a 49ers secondary that has utilized single high at the eighth-highest rate (57.7%). Since Week 2, against single high, Sutton has had only an 18% target per route run rate and 1.57 YPRR. Last year, he crushed single high with a 26% target per route run rate and 2.32 YPRR. It's asking a lot of Nix to support multiple pass catchers at the moment, but if Nix can snap out of his funk, Sutton does have some flex value in a tough matchup. The 49ers have allowed the sixth-fewest yards per target and the seventh-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

After three games, Kalif Raymond is the WR14 in fantasy points per game. His usage looks real, and we should all stand up and take notice. Raymond has a 20.4% target share with 2.85 YPRR, three red zone targets, one deep target, and a 23% first-read share (second on the team). We'll see if he keeps this up, but he looks legit. This week, he faces a Jets' secondary that has the fifth-highest two-high rate in the NFL (65.4%). Against two-high, Raymond leads the team with a 22% target-per-route run rate with 2.00 YPRR. Raymond is a solid flex with a tougher matchup. New York has allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 17th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed.

This is what Tre Tucker does. He pops off with the occasional big game, and then fantasy gamers are left chasing that high. Last week, Tucker came back to earth. In Weeks 1 and 3, Tucker has had only a 12.7% target share, 1.30 YPRR, one red zone target, zero deep targets, and a 15% first-read share. None of these metrics are anything to write home about. This week, he faces a Kansas City secondary that has held perimeter wide receivers to the third-fewest yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity. Tucker is an easy sit.

The Bills' passing attack has flowed through DJ Moore and Dalton Kincaid this season, which has left Khalil Shakir on the outside looking in. Shakir is the WR75 in fantasy points per game. He has a 16.4% target share, 1.37 YPRR, four red zone targets, zero deep targets, and an 18.5% first-read share. Shakir is a sit this week. New England has allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target to slot receivers. Yes, they have given up two receiving scores to slot receivers, but they both came last week, with Parker Washington and Josh Cameron getting into the end zone.

Xavier Worthy's role cratered last week. After fighting for second or third in the target pecking order over the previous games, Worthy fell to the bottom of the pile with an 8.3% target share, 1.06 YPRR, zero red-zone and deep targets, and a 5.6% first-read share (last among the Chiefs starters). Worthy is an easy sit this week. The Raiders have allowed the fewest yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Over the last two games, Mack Hollins has led the Patriots with a 20.8% target share with 2.39 YPRR, three red zone targets, a deep target, and a 26.5% first-read share. These are strong usage and production metrics across the board. Hollins is a solid flex play this week, although I don't know if he'll retain his top spot in the passing attack in Week 4. Buffalo has the tenth-highest two-high rate (58.1%). Since Week 2, against two-high, Hollins has been second on the team with a 17% target-per-route run rate with a stellar 2.46 YPRR. Since 2025, against two-high, Hollins has had a 19% target-per-route run rate and 2.05 YPRR against two-high. Buffalo is 15th in yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity allowed to perimeter wide receivers.

Despite posting a struggle bus stat line last week, Michael Pittman Jr. had a 70.3% route share, so he was close to a full-time player for the Steelers on passing plays. Pittman has had a sleepy start to his Steelers career with a 10.7% target share, 1.19 YPRR, zero deep or red zone targets, and a 9.1% first-read share. Sit Pittman again this week. After their Week 1 debacle, the Browns' secondary has tightened up, allowing the seventh-fewest yards per target and the fifth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers over the last two weeks.

Rashod Bateman returned to the shadow realm last week with Zay Flowers active. In the two games this season that Flowers has played, Bateman has had an 8.9% target share with 0.80 YPRR, one red zone target, zero deep targets, and a 12.1% first-read share. Bateman is essentially Flowers' handcuff. He's a must-sit with Flowers back in the lineup.

Chris Godwin has looked cooked through three games as the WR59 in fantasy points per game. Godwin has an 11.1% target share with 1.14 YPRR, zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 14.5% first-read share. Among 86 qualifying receivers, he ranks 57th in separation and 49th in route win rate. This week, he faces a Green Bay pass defense that has the sixth-highest two-high rate (64.4%). Against two-high, Godwin has only an 8% target-per-route run rate and 0.33 YPRR. Sit Godwin this week. Green Bay has allowed the tenth-fewest yards per target to slot receivers while ranking 17th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed.

There's no way I'm playing Quentin Johnston in any league this week. Johnston has only a 17% target share with 0.79 YPRR and a 22% first-read share. Johnston leads the team with three deep targets, but he has zero red zone targets. Seattle has allowed the fourth-fewest yards per target and the tenth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Brian Thomas Jr. has had a predictable but rough beginning to the season. Last week, his route share dipped to 43.8% while he had only a 3.4% target share. Thomas Jr. is an easy sit this week with his role declining in the Jags offense and possible shadow coverage from DJ Turner when he's on the field. I don't know if Cincy will view Jakobi Meyers as the bigger threat this week or Thomas Jr., but Cincy has also been tough against perimeter receivers. Thomas Jr. is a sit, regardless of how you dice up this matchup. Turner has shadowed in each game this season following Emeka Egbuka, Xavier Hutchinson, and DK Metcalf on 53.1-69% of their routes. Turner hasn't allowed any of these receivers to surpass 53 receiving yards in his coverage. Metcalf scored a touchdown against him, but Turner ran into a teammate on the play, which left Metcalf wide open. Cincy has allowed the second-fewest yards per target and the fourth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

At this point, the Cards should trade Marvin Harrison Jr. He isn't part of the offensive game plan weekly, with only a 6.8% target share (18.6 aDOT) and 9.1% first-read share. Harrison Jr. is just running clear-out routes for the rest of the pass catchers on the depth chart. He's droppable.
Jalen Coker sustained a quad injury last week. He opened this week with a DNP. I'll update his outlook on Friday.

Makai Lemon is still just a stash-and-hold player for fantasy purposes. He hasn't had more than three receptions and 29 receiving yards in any game this season. Overall, he has an 80.2% route share (83.9% last week), a 10.2% target share, 0.45 YPRR, zero red zone targets, one deep target, and a 12.5% first-read share. Over the last two weeks, Lemon has seen aDOTs of 14.0 and 11.7 with slot rates of 48.4% and 73.1%. This situation for Lemon remains a work in progress. Stash him until the usage changes.
